title: Micro-latency Token Coalescer and Preemptive Flush Spec
content:
Context and motivation:
This is a working spec for a small, low-latency coalescing layer inside the serving runtime that sits between the token generator (kernel outputs / kv cache readback) and the network emission layer (HTTP/HTTP2/WS streaming output). The goal: reduce per-token RPC overhead while honoring tight latency SLOs for interactive applications and enabling preemptive flush/cancellation semantics that behave well when higher-priority requests arrive or a user cancels mid-stream.

Why this doc: existing streaming drafts cover chunking and eviction at a coarse grain, but we see repeated customer feedback that per-token jitter and micro-latency spikes (2-30ms) cause bad UX in editor-type apps. We also need a clear contract between the runtime scheduler (which decides kernel scheduling/batching) and the emission layer so that KV-cache replays and partial-token boundaries never double-send or leak inconsistent state.

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
- Keep tail latency for first bytes under 60ms for 95th p95 across normal requests (configurable per-profile).
- Reduce small-message overhead: coalesce multiple tiny token emissions into a single network frame when safe, without adding perceptible latency to the user.
- Provide deterministic preemption: when a higher-priority request must be serviced (or a cancellation event), be able to flush or abort in-flight partial tokens with minimal duplication or ordering anomalies.
- Preserve correctness with KV cache: tokens emitted that depend on a KV read should not be duplicated or replayed incorrectly when cache-misses/hits occur.
- Be lightweight and easy to opt-in/out per route/model.

Core concepts and primitives:
1) Emission unit (EU): the minimal atomic payload the network layer can accept. Typically an EU is 1 token, but can be logical fragments when models emit sub-token pieces (partial UTF-8 bytes) or user-level code maps tokens into strings. We treat EU as an opaque byte payload + metadata: {request_id, seq_no, token_boundary, kv_epoch}.

2) Coalescer window: a short-duration sliding window (default 8ms) where EUs are buffered and then batched into one outbound frame. Window is tunable per route: low-latency routes use 0–2ms, interactive editor routes 8–15ms, background batch routes 50–200ms.

3) Flush triggers: events that cause an immediate emission of buffered EUs. Examples:
- Window timer expiry (normal case)
- Forced flush from scheduler due to preemption/higher-priority request arrival
- Cancellation from client (client wants an ACK that cancellation observed)
- Network backpressure change (e.g., socket drain/writable)
- Full-batch size reached (byte or EU count)

4) Token boundary semantics: if the model emits partial bytes for a physical token, we track token_boundary flags. The coalescer must avoid sending incomplete UTF-8 sequences as standalone frames unless the client has indicated it can handle byte-stream partials (flag in request). Default behavior is to buffer partial bytes until token boundary or until a hard flush event occurs; in the latter case, annotate frame with "partial_token": true so clients can decide how to render.

5) KV epoch coupling: every EU includes kv_epoch (a monotonic id representing the version of KV state read by the kernel). If a cached prefix is later evicted and regenerated with different epoch, the runtime uses kv_epoch to prevent accidental duplication in replay scenarios: network frames include epoch metadata, and on retransmit the system can choose to drop earlier EUs with mismatched epoch for idempotency.

Algorithm (simplified):
- On kernel output: convert kernel output to one or more EUs, annotate with seq_no (per-request increment), token_boundary and kv_epoch. Push into per-request coalescer queue.
- If coalescer window not running, start timer with interval = route.window_ms (unless route.mode = "immediate").
- On timer fire or flush trigger: create frame from queued EUs up to max_bytes. For each EU marked partial_token and route.partial_disallowed => keep it in queue if not forced flush. If forced flush and partial exists, mark frame.partial_token = true and include note in metadata.
- Mark frame with last_seq_sent. Append frame to network egress buffer.
- On preemptive scheduler flush: scheduler signals the coalescer with a preemptive hint (higher_priority_request_id). Coalescer must decide: if fewer than Xms elapsed since EU arrival, batch them (if priority tolerance allows), else immediate flush and attach preemption metadata so downstream aggregators (load balancer, multiplexer) can reorder/merge with minimal head-of-line blocking.

Cancellation model:
- Client may send cancel request or close connection. We want to guarantee a clear predicate: either the server sends an explicit cancellation-ack frame ("cancel-ack" with last_seq_received) or the server simply tears down the stream with reason="cancelled-by-client".
- If cancel arrives while coalescer is holding partial_token and no frame has been emitted: on cancel, coalescer does one of two modes (configurable per route):
  * "best-effort-ack": flush partial as partial_token frame then emit cancel-ack.
  * "strict-rollback": drop partials and emit cancel-ack referencing previous seq.
- Recommendation: default to best-effort-ack for interactive routes, strict-rollback for financial/legal routes.

Preemption and higher-priority arrivals:
- When a higher-priority kernel needs immediate GPU time and we preempt current request, we follow this sequence:
  1) Scheduler requests cooperative preemption from the request's coalescer.
  2) Coalescer has short timeout (preemption_timeout_ms, default 4ms) to flush buffered EUs. If it cannot flush because of partial_token that cannot be safely sent, scheduler can either: a) wait additional grace period (up to 10ms) b) forcibly interrupt kernel and accept partial_token emission with metadata c) migrate KV/seq state and resume later (complex).
  3) Preemption metadata contains preempted_by request id and preempt_seq_no so the consumer can reason about continuity.
- Important: preemption must not violate per-request in-order token delivery. If preemption causes reordering at the client (e.g., preempted request's final frame arrives after higher-priority response), upstream multiplexer must preserve per-request sequencing and avoid cross-request interleaving.

KV cache correctness notes:
- Kernel outputs that depend on KV cache lookups include kv_epoch. If a coalescer flush is emitted but later the kernel is rolled back due to cache revalidation and re-execution, the system must correlate frames using request_id+seq_no+kv_epoch to avoid delivering stale tokens. Practical approach: maintain a short soft-retention window (configurable, default 2s) where emitted frames are retained and marked as reversible until final commit. If rollback occurs within window, emit a "retract" frame referencing seq_no(s). Client libraries can use retract to remove tokens.
- Retract is messy for many clients. Alternative: make kernel commit on KV read-path before emission when possible (adds 1-2ms) or accept eventual consistency at UI layer. Recommend opt-in per route.

Kernel and scheduling considerations (what scheduler needs from coalescer):
- Visibility into coalescer queue length and oldest EU age (metrics): coalescer should export e.g., pending_eus, oldest_eu_ms to scheduler for smarter decisions.
- Fast signal to request cooperative yield (preemptive hint) and feedback if flush could not complete in preemption window.
- Ability to lock emission for short critical sections (e.g., when emitting tokens that must be contiguous and tied to atomic kernel state) — but use sparingly.

Metrics & observability:
- per-route: avg_coalesce_latency_ms, p95_coalesce_latency_ms, flush_count_by_trigger (timer/forced/preempt/cancel), partial_token_flush_rate, retract_count, preempt_flush_failures
- per-request: eu_count, last_seq_emitted, kv_epoch_at_emit, cancel_ack_latency
- Traces: end-to-end span from kernel-output->coalescer->network-send with tags for preempted/cancelled/partial.

Open questions / tradeoffs / TODOs:
- Retract vs rollback cost: what fraction of customer routes want retract semantics? Need experiment and telemetry sampling.
- Default window sizing by model family and route type — heuristics to explore: concatenate median token duration (kernel) + network RTT to choose window.
- UX for partial_token frames: standardize client-side rendering conventions; propose default UI show spinner for partials and patch when completed.
- Backpressure interactions with HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE and WebSocket - what is precedence when network becomes non-writable? Should coalescer keep buffering indefinitely? (no) propose max_buffer_ms = 500ms then apply backpressure up the scheduler.
- Security: retract frames may be confusing for logs/audit trails—ensure audit log includes all emitted frames even if retracted.

Experiment plan (short):
- Week 1: implement coalescer with window_ms configurable; route-level toggles; basic timer+forced-flush handling. Add metrics and a feature-flag.
- Week 2: run A/B on 10% traffic of interactive editor routes comparing window_ms=8ms vs 0ms (immediate). Measure p50/p95 latency and client-side perceived jitter.
- Week 3: add preemptive hint path, simulate high-priority preemption load and measure kernel scheduling improvements and any duplicate/partial emission rates.
- Week 4: evaluate retract complexity on small set of traffic where strict consistency required.

Appendix: short state machine (imperative wording)
- States: Idle, Buffering, Emitting, Preempted, Draining, Cancelled
- Transitions:
  * Idle->Buffering on first EU arrive, start window timer
  * Buffering->Emitting on timer or forced flush
  * Buffering->Preempted on preempt hint; if can flush within preempt_timeout -> Emitting, else Draining (force partial if allowed)
  * Emitting->Idle when egress confirmed or queue empty
  * Any->Cancelled on cancel event

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally light on formal proofs; focus is practical engineering tradeoffs. Please comment on the preemption_timeout defaults, retract semantics, and KV coupling. If you have a client rendering story for partial tokens, paste examples.

References and linked artifacts: JIRA-RT-998 (scheduler preemption epic), CON-1245 (kv cache epochs design), https://confluence.redwood.ai/serving/runtime/kv-cache-notes
